chapter_title: Chương 279: Lời bộc bạch về bạch kim

segments.title: Chương 279: Lời bộc bạch về bạch kim
segments.content:
Life is like a dream, sometimes it feels quite surreal.

The first time I learned of the existence of Platinum Authors was when I was reading a book by an author named Xě Hóng. The first time I wanted to make money writing web novels was also after learning that Xě Hóng was already making millions a year back in 2005.

My thanks to Big Boss Xě Hóng, though I've never spoken with him or had any dealings with him.

When you're young, you like to dream. When you're a bit older, you like to reminisce. I, too, have reached the age where I like to reminisce, and I understand why so many people like to publish their memoirs.

The high school portion of this book contains a lot of beautified memories of reality.

I didn't have much access to books as a child, so I did enjoy picking through garbage heaps to find things to read. To be precise, they weren't even books, but all sorts of scraps of paper with words on them.

My dad was a migrant worker. I don't know where he got them, but he had a whole drawer full of books. They were a motley collection, everything from cookbooks to who knows what else.

Before I could even read, my favorite was the *Zuo Zhuan*. Because it was the thickest book, and it was typeset vertically from right to left, unlike all the other books.

I would pretend to read the *Zuo Zhuan* when I had nothing else to do, and from it, I learned the character "之" (zhī). It was the first character I ever learned, as it appeared quite frequently in the *Zuo Zhuan*.

The first wuxia I ever read was Wolong Sheng's *The Fugitive*, but it was a tattered, incomplete copy with missing pages.

The second wuxia was Jin Yong's *The Heaven Sword and Dragon Saber*, in even worse condition.

Kids nowadays like to play with cigarette packs, and we had a similar game back then. But we used cardboard folded from torn book pages.

At the time, a kid tore up *The Heaven Sword and Dragon Saber* and folded it into cardboard pieces, and I won a good number of them through the game. I unfolded them one by one, rearranged them by page number, and sewed them together with a needle and thread.

It was missing the beginning and the end, and the pages often skipped, but I read it with great relish, guessing and piecing things together.

Back then I was still in elementary school, and I felt that having books to read was a special kind of happiness.

Once, in junior high, I went to the county seat with an older boy from my village. Outside his school, I discovered for the first time that book rental shops existed. I rented a set of *Yang Xiaoxie*, but I only had one weekend to read it, because I had to ask him to return it for me when he went back to school.

I remember it so clearly: two days and one night, I did nothing but read that novel, except to eat. It was the middle of summer, but I didn't even take a shower. When one eye got tired, I'd close it and use the other.

In high school, my reading became even more frantic. I'd rent six thick, pirated novels a day, and I almost never studied seriously. My grades plummeted, and it just so happened to be the year of the disastrous Sichuan college entrance exams in '06. In a daze, I ended up in some undergraduate program, just getting by.

During university, I was also reading and writing novels. Unfortunately, I lacked talent and couldn't produce anything noteworthy.

I only started to panic after graduation, having no idea what I could do.

I bought a recruitment newspaper off the street, and in a muddle, I joined a newly-opened company. I helped the boss clean the office and went with her to purchase office computers.

The boss was a menopausal woman of about 50, both stingy and pedantic. When she went to get business cards printed, she could drive the print shop staff to the point of quitting on the spot.

In less than three months, only the driver and I were left in the company; all the other employees had resigned. Then, on my monthly salary of 2500 yuan, I first took on the roles of both accountant and cashier, then became responsible for recruiting new employees. I also had to get the business license renewed, file taxes, and open an online banking account for the company.

Gradually, I also became the computer and network maintenance guy, though my skills were not even on par with a network administrator. I also became the purchasing agent, buying things like roll-up banners for exhibitions. Then I became the operations director, supervising the outsourced team running around everywhere.

The company also took on a magazine affiliated with the Ministry of Transport, and a department director even came to hold a meeting and provide guidance. Transport law enforcement departments from all over the country would send their manuscripts to me, and I would be the sole editor. Even a few years ago, an old colleague from a transport department would still, for some reason, occasionally send me manuscripts out of the blue.

I also became a debt collector. The boss sent me to collect a final payment. I camped out in the office of the director of the Banking Regulatory Commission's Shancheng office for half a month. I successfully wore him down and got the final payment.

Back then, if the graphic designer was away, I even had to step in as a temporary art editor.

Truthfully, I didn't know anything. I had to learn every task on the fly. The boss kept piling on the work, and I kept learning new things.

You never know your own potential until you're pushed.

And yet, my salary remained just 2500 yuan.

There wasn't even a year-end bonus. At the end of the year, she even had me go out and deliver shopping cards to people as kickbacks.

After I delivered the kickbacks, I came back to the company and found there was nothing for me. She even went back on her verbal promise of a project commission.

It was the first time I realized just how shameless a capitalist could be.

After the New Year, I returned to the company to resign.

The boss tried her best to persuade me to stay, saying she would give me a raise, but without giving one immediately.

I thanked my boss, then turned around and encouraged the employees I had recruited myself to resign. Within a month, the company was once again left with only the boss and the driver.

Then I started writing novels full-time. After more than half a year, my total income from royalties was just over 500 yuan. At my poorest, I had to borrow money to pay rent.

I had no choice but to go look for a job again.

The new job was as an editor for a photography newspaper. The boss was someone I had met when I was doing sales. He started the newspaper to sell liquor, and only to government agencies.

The salary was 3500 yuan, and I was in charge of the entire newspaper by myself. That included the work of a graphic designer.

The new boss promised that as long as I finished one issue of the paper each month, I could manage my own time. I could even edit the manuscripts from my rented apartment while working.

Never believe the words of a capitalist. The more capable you appear, the more work will be waiting for you. I even had to accompany the boss to social events, to drink with a bunch of government officials.

The boss said he was grooming me. I was very grateful for his grooming, so I worked long enough to earn a few months' rent and then resigned.

And I went back to writing novels full-time.

I truly have no talent. I just kept writing, kept pushing through, and before I knew it, more than ten years had passed.

Of the old authors who started writing around the same time as me, there aren't many left now.

Being cooped up at home typing all year round makes a person more and more withdrawn. I can't even be bothered to look at QQ or WeChat, and I'm very resistant to communicating with people.

It wasn't until I went to a Qidian event the year before last that I found out my group's editor-in-chief was a beautiful woman. I had always called her "Laoda" and thought she was a man.

Really? I don't believe it, not unless there's a picture. This time, being suddenly promoted to Platinum, I was honestly a bit overwhelmed. Because I really haven't achieved much, and I've had almost no communication with my editor.

Just like with getting into university and finding a job, this promotion to Platinum also happened in a daze.

Life is like a dream. It's rare to be muddled, I suppose.
